section_title: What happens when the threat returns after a word of reassurance?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 When the Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish, he withdrew and found the king fighting against Libnah. 9 Now Sennacherib had been warned about Tirhakah king of Cush: “He has set out to fight against you.” On hearing this, Sennacherib sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying,

10 “Give this message to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. 11 Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other countries, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be spared? 12 Did the gods of the nations destroyed by my fathers rescue those nations—the gods of Gozan, Haran, and Rezeph, and of the people of Eden in Telassar? 13 Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’”

context_lines: The Rabshakeh returns and finds Sennacherib fighting at Libnah after leaving Lachish. News arrives that Tirhakah king of Cush has set out against him. Sennacherib then sends another message to Hezekiah.

This time the challenge directly accuses the God Hezekiah trusts of deceiving him. The letter lists defeated lands and asks whether Jerusalem can expect a different outcome. The Assyrian record of conquest is made to sound like proof that no deliverance is possible.

The passage continues the pressure rather than resolving it. Hezekiah has received the Lord’s promise, yet another threatening message still arrives. His response to that letter follows in verses 14–20.
common_interpretation_lines: [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/37.htm) reads the renewed message as an attempt to force a quick surrender while another military concern presses upon Sennacherib. He notes that interpreters differ over which report is meant by the earlier promise that the king would hear a rumor.

[Henry’s treatment of the parallel account](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_kings/19.htm) places this renewed threat beside the prayer it prompts. The enemy’s message becomes the occasion for Hezekiah to bring the matter to God, rather than accept the enemy’s verdict as final.
These explanations follow the movement of the narrative: another danger does not cancel the promise, but it does test how Hezekiah will respond to the words he has received.
